## Objectives

By the end of today you will be able to:

1. Save a value in an object with `<-` and use it later.
2. Choose good object names.
3. Tell the four basic data types apart: numeric, character, logical and factor.
4. Convert a value from one type to another.
5. Recognise missing values (`NA`) and work around them.

## Saving values in objects

On Day 1 every result disappeared as soon as R printed it. To keep a value, give it a name with the **assignment arrow** `<-`:

```{webr}
price <- 2500
price
```

Read `<-` as "gets": "`price` gets 2500". The name `price` now points to the value 2500. R calls this an **object**. You can use it anywhere you would use the number:

```{webr}
price * 3
total <- price * 3 + 800
total
```

If you assign a new value to the same name, the old one is replaced:

```{webr}
price <- 3000
price
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Excel bridge
An object is like a named cell. In Excel you might name cell B2 `price` and write `=price*3`. In R you write `price * 3`. The difference is that R objects can hold far more than one number, as you will see tomorrow.
:::

### Naming rules

- Names can contain letters, numbers, `.` and `_`, but must start with a letter.
- R is case-sensitive: `Price` and `price` are different objects.
- Use names that say what the value is: `monthly_rent` is better than `x2`.
- Most R users write names in `snake_case`: lower-case words joined by `_`.

## The four basic data types

Every value in R has a type. The type decides what you can do with it. Use `class()` to check:

```{webr}
class(42.5)        # numeric: numbers
class("Kampala")   # character: text
class(TRUE)        # logical: TRUE or FALSE
```

### Numeric

Numbers, with or without decimals. You can do maths with them.

### Character

Text, always written inside quotes. You cannot do maths with text, even if it looks like a number:

```{webr}
"5" + 1 # Error expected: "5" is text, not a number
```

### Logical

Only two values: `TRUE` and `FALSE`. You get logical values when you compare things:

```{webr}
10 > 3
10 == 3     # == means "is equal to". A single = is not a comparison.
10 != 3     # != means "is not equal to"
"a" == "a"
```

Logical values are the basis of filtering data, which you will do from Day 3 onwards.

### Factor

A factor is a category with a fixed set of possible values, called **levels**. Survey answers such as "Agree", "Neutral" and "Disagree" are a typical example.

```{webr}
answer <- factor("Agree", levels = c("Disagree", "Neutral", "Agree"))
answer
levels(answer)
```

You will use factors much more on Day 11. For now, recognise one when you see it.

## Converting between types

Data often arrives with the wrong type. A number read from a file may be stored as text. Convert it with an `as.` function:

```{webr}
as.numeric("5") + 1
as.character(2026)
as.logical("TRUE")
```

If R cannot convert a value, it gives `NA` and a warning:

```{webr}
as.numeric("five")
```

## Missing values: NA

`NA` means "not available": the value is missing. It is not zero and it is not blank. It means "unknown".

Anything calculated from an unknown value is also unknown:

```{webr}
NA + 10
NA > 5
```

Use `is.na()` to test for a missing value. You cannot use `== NA`, because the answer to "is this unknown thing equal to an unknown thing?" is also unknown:

```{webr}
age <- NA
age == NA    # gives NA, not TRUE
is.na(age)   # the right way
```

Many functions have an argument `na.rm = TRUE` ("remove NAs") that skips missing values. You will use it on Day 3.

## Exercises

### Exercise 1: Create and use objects

A household spends 450,000 shillings a month on rent. Create an object called `rent` with that value. Then calculate the cost for a whole year.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex2_rent
rent <- ______
rent * ______
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex2_rent"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
Put the number after `<-`. A year has 12 months.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex2_rent"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
rent <- 450000
rent * 12
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex2_rent
#| check: true
if (!exists("rent")) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Create an object called rent with <-.")
} else if (!isTRUE(all.equal(rent, 450000))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "rent should be 450000. Do not use commas inside numbers in R.")
} else if (isTRUE(all.equal(.result, 5400000))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct: 5,400,000 shillings a year.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "rent is right. Now multiply it by the number of months in a year.")
}
```

### Exercise 2: Check the type

What type is the value `"2026"`? Use a function to find out.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex2_class
______("2026")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex2_class"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
The function that reports a type is `class()`. Notice the quotes around `2026`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex2_class"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
class("2026")
```
It is `"character"`. The quotes make it text, even though it looks like a number.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex2_class
#| check: true
if (identical(.result, "character")) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Right. The quotes make it text.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Use class() on the value exactly as written, with the quotes.")
}
```

### Exercise 3: Fix the type

The object `score` came from a file and is stored as text. Convert it to a number, then add 10.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex2_convert
#| setup: true
score <- "85"
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex2_convert
______(score) + 10
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex2_convert"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
The `as.` function for numbers is `as.numeric()`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex2_convert"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
as.numeric(score) + 10
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex2_convert
#| check: true
if (isTRUE(all.equal(.result, 95))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct: 95.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Convert score with as.numeric() before adding 10.")
}
```

### Exercise 4: Compare values

Is `budget` greater than or equal to `cost`? Write a comparison that answers `TRUE` or `FALSE`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex2_compare
#| setup: true
budget <- 120000
cost <- 118500
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex2_compare
budget ______ cost
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex2_compare"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
"Greater than or equal to" is written `>=`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex2_compare"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
budget >= cost
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex2_compare
#| check: true
if (identical(.result, TRUE)) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct. The budget covers the cost.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "You should get TRUE. Use >= between the two objects.")
}
```

### Exercise 5: Test for a missing value

The object `income` may be missing. Write code that returns `TRUE` if it is missing.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex2_na
#| setup: true
income <- NA
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex2_na
______(income)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex2_na"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint
`income == NA` does not work. There is a special function for this.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex2_na"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
is.na(income)
```
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex2_na
#| check: true
if (identical(.result, TRUE)) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct. Always use is.na() to find missing values.")
} else if (identical(.result, NA)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "You got NA. That happens with == NA. Use is.na() instead.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Use is.na() on income.")
}
```

## Common mistakes

- **Using `=` to compare.** `x = 5` assigns. `x == 5` compares.
- **Commas in numbers.** Write `450000`, not `450,000`. R reads the comma as a separator.
- **Quotes around numbers.** `"85"` is text. You cannot do maths with it until you convert it.
- **Testing for missing values with `==`.** Use `is.na(x)`.
- **Spaces inside the arrow.** `x < - 5` means "is x less than minus 5?". Write `x <- 5`.

## Summary

- `<-` saves a value in an object: `price <- 2500`.
- Good names are short, clear and in `snake_case`.
- The basic types are numeric, character (text), logical (`TRUE`/`FALSE`) and factor (categories). Check a type with `class()`.
- Convert types with `as.numeric()`, `as.character()` and `as.logical()`.
- `NA` is a missing value. Test for it with `is.na()`.

**Tomorrow:** you will store many values in one object, called a vector.
